The Italian agile frog, Rana latastei, exhibits a distinct set of life-history traits shaped by its reliance on ephemeral woodland pools. Oviposition occurs during early spring, with females depositing clutches in shallow, cool water. Field studies have shown that eclosion of the jelly-coated eggs typically occurs after about 12 days [ab = about 12 days] when water temperatures remain near 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The freshly emerged yolk-sac larva, or pre-feeding tadpole, is minute, with an estimated wet weight at birth of only 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams]. This endotrophic stage relies entirely on internal yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Following the trophic switch to active feeding, the aquatic tadpole enters a period of rapid growth. The subsequent larval-juvenile transition, or metamorphic climax, is a critical bottleneck. Under consistent thermal conditions of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 76 days , at which point the snout-vent length (SVL) of the newly terrestrial froglet is remarkably consistent, measuring about 1.3 centimeters .

Sexual maturation in Rana latastei is closely tied to body size rather than a strict chronological age, though a minimum developmental period is required. In populations inhabiting cooler, shaded breeding sites where water temperatures average 7 °C [T = 7 °C], both sexes typically attain puberty after a prolonged juvenile phase. At the onset of gonadal maturation, or puberty, the snout-vent length of individuals is quite uniform, with frogs measuring about 3.5 centimeters [Lp = about 3.5 centimeters] at this life stage. This size threshold appears critical; reaching it before the onset of winter is a major determinant of whether an individual will breed in its second spring or must delay reproduction for an additional year.

Adult body size in Rana latastei shows a modest degree of sexual dimorphism, with females attaining larger ultimate dimensions than males. Extensive field surveys using mark-recapture methods have documented the ultimate snout-vent length for females at 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], representing the maximum size achieved in natural populations. Consistent with the general pattern observed across many ranid frogs, males are slightly smaller, with the ultimate SVL for males being 7.3 centimeters [Li = 7.3 centimeters]. This size divergence is also reflected in body mass; gravid females, which invest heavily in egg production, can reach an ultimate wet weight of 39.5 grams [Wwi = 39.5 grams]. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males is somewhat lower, estimated at 36.4 grams [Wwi = 36.4 grams]. This sexual size dimorphism likely influences mating dynamics, with larger females being more fecund and dominant males potentially securing more amplexus opportunities.

The maximum lifespan of Rana latastei in its native lowland forests of northern Italy is relatively modest for an anuran. Based on long-term monitoring of individually marked cohorts, the oldest documented individuals in the wild reach an age of about 5 years [am = about 5 years], when exposed to average annual thermal conditions near 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, typical of temperate-zone ranids, imposes a strong selective pressure for early and efficient reproduction. Females are capable of producing only a single clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs per year], a constraint that limits their lifetime reproductive output. However, within that single annual event, fecundity is substantial; clutch sizes range from 676 to 2,720 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 676 to 2,720 eggs per clutch]. This high fecundity, coupled with a low survival probability for eggs and larvae, is characteristic of a classic boom-bust reproductive strategy. Collectively, this translates into a daily reproduction rate of about 3.5 eggs per day when averaged over the entire year.

Reproductive investment in the Italian agile frog is highly sensitive to environmental temperature, which governs the pace of embryonic and larval development. At a constant incubation temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], laboratory studies have documented the maximum possible reproductive rate for this species, which equates to approximately 3.5 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 3.5 eggs per day] when averaged across the entire year. This high potential output is rarely realized in the wild, as spring temperatures are often lower and more variable than this optimal benchmark. The thermal dependency of early life stages is particularly acute. The time since birth at metamorphosis, for instance, is drastically extended under cooler conditions; at a constant 7 °C [T = 7 °C], development to metamorphosis requires roughly 76 days , a period that exposes tadpoles to prolonged predation risk from aquatic insects and newts. This strong thermal constraint on growth rates and the timing of the terrestrial transition is a primary driver of population dynamics in this ephemeral-pond specialist.
